scenario: AITA for asking my pregnant SIL to leave the family Christmas gathering? | Okay so based on title I totally sound like an asshole but hear me out. So this year is our turn to host the family Christmas party at our home. We invited not only my SOs side but also my side as well. Overall it was around 20ish people in our home today for gift giving and typical American Christmas celebrating. Drinks were shared, food broken, the whole shebang. Amongst my SOs side of the family was his pregnant sister. She, I think, was due maybe a week or so ago? But really its just been ticking time bomb for her little one to arrive. Everybodys excited to meet the baby! Now our problem is that SIL came to the party with contractions and was obviously in labor (I know this because Im a mom myself - once you know, you know). Every 20 minutes or so she would start having pains and would make noises to pass the contractions. At first it wasnt so bad; I understand how sucky it is and you dont want to go to the hospital too soon because they'll just send you right home. But then it became almost obnoxious. I feel terrible for saying that but it really was. A lot of my family members and some of hers were glancing around like WTF? Go home and do that in private. After a while it became apparent that it was making everybody uncomfortable and even my MIL reccommend that she rest at home before it gets too late. She refused and said she was fine. In the middle of the kids opening their presents she went into pain again and this time she even screamed for a second. I then discreetly pulled her husband to the side and told them to leave. I did it politely ("Hey I appreciate you guys for being here but I think its time to go. I dont want you guys to give birth in our kitchen! lol"). After I said that her husband got angry and quickly got her and the kids packed up. She visibly upset and before heading out called me a bitch and said that I ruined Christmas for her. A few of their sides family members gave me dirty looks and left soon after. Im torn on this: I wanted everybody to have a good day but it was very distracting and obnoxious to have her around. I feel bad but still. tl;dr -- I asked SIL to leave family Christmas party because she was in labor.

Even if it was uncomfortable for others, her bodily autonomy and emotional well-being matter. While it’s reasonable to expect guests to behave in a way that doesn’t disrupt the event, labor is an unpredictable and unavoidable medical situation. Your SIL’s husband’s anger suggests that he felt his wife’s needs weren’t being respected, which is a valid concern. Had you handled it differently (e.g., offering to help her leave quietly, or even suggesting she use a private space in your home), it might have gone smoother. 4. **Cultural Norms and Gender Dynamics:** - Pregnancy and childbirth are often stigmatized or treated as "private" matters, especially in conservative or traditional settings. Your SIL’s outburst ("you ruined Christmas for me") reflects how deeply personal this experience is to her. Women (and pregnant people) are often expected to endure discomfort in social settings, and your request to leave may have felt like an extension of that pressure. 5. **Long-Term Relationship Impact:** - Your SIL’s reaction (and her family’s) suggests this could strain relationships. Labor is disruptive, and no one wants to witness it in a social setting. - **From an ethical standpoint:** It was **wrong** to ask her to leave without considering her emotional state, her husband’s feelings, or the broader context of her vulnerability. The way you framed it ("don’t give birth in our kitchen") was tone-deaf and could be seen as mocking or dismissive. ### **How Could It Have Been Handled Better?** 1. **Private Intervention:** - Instead of addressing her in front of others, discreetly pull her husband aside (as you did) and say something like: *"Hey, I know this is a tough time, but I’m worried about her comfort and the energy of the party. Would you like to step out for a bit? We can help you get settled somewhere quiet if you’d like."* - This acknowledges her situation while offering support. 2. **Offering Space:** - If she refused to leave, you could have suggested a private area (e.g., a guest room, basement, or even a quiet corner) where she could rest without disrupting the gathering. This shows consideration without forcing her to leave. 3. **Avoiding Humor:** - The "don’t give birth in our kitchen" line came across as flippant. Labor is serious, and humor about it can feel insensitive, especially when someone is in pain. 4. **Apologizing Later:** - If you believe you overstepped, a sincere apology (not to her, but to her husband or family) could help mitigate the fallout. For example: *"I realize now that I could have handled this better. I didn’t mean to make things harder for you—just wanted everyone to have a good time."* ### **Final Thought:** This situation highlights how family gatherings can become fraught when personal and social expectations collide. While your intentions were likely good (preserving the party’s atmosphere), the way you handled it prioritized the group’s comfort over an individual’s immediate needs. **The right thing would have been to balance both—acknowledging her labor while trying to minimize disruption in a way that didn’t feel dismissive.** Would you like help brainstorming how to repair the relationship moving forward?
